title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
keywords: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal
Frivaldo v. Comelec and Sinaca v. Mula
primary_topics: Chapter 19 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's analysis of Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (GR 142840, May 7, 2001, per Kapunan, J.), holding that repatriation under RA 2630 restores a person's ORIGINAL citizenship, so that a natural-born Filipino who lost his status and was repatriated reacquires natural-born (not merely naturalized) citizenship

The facts: Teodoro C. Cruz, natural-born in 1960, lost his Philippine citizenship by enlisting in the US Marine Corps and being naturalized American, then repatriated in 1994 and was elected to the House from Pangasinan; the HRET upheld his qualifications, and Antonio Bengson III's certiorari petition charged the HRET with grave abuse

The ruling's logic: there are only two classes of citizens -- natural-born and naturalized -- and since Cruz did not reacquire citizenship by naturalization or a direct act of Congress, he 'necessarily is a natural-born Filipino'; the Constitution provides no separate category for those who reacquire citizenship

CJP's Concurring Opinion (originally a dissent he converted after deferring to the senior Justice Kapunan), giving five reasons -- repatriation as recovery of original citizenship; not-naturalized-therefore-natural-born; no grave abuse by the HRET as 'sole judge' of qualifications; popular will prevails in case of doubt; and the trend toward globalization -- against Justice Gutierrez's dissent that natural-born status, once lost, cannot be reacquired
sub_topics: The question: what does repatriation under RA 2630 reacquire -- the 'original' citizenship previously lost, or 'an entirely new one'? -- and specifically whether a person who lost natural-born status reacquires natural-born citizenship

The facts: Teodoro C. Cruz, born April 27, 1960 in San Clemente, Tarlac of Filipino parents (natural-born under the 1935 Constitution), enlisted in the US Marine Corps and took a US oath on November 5, 1985 (losing citizenship under CA 63, Section 1(4)), was naturalized American on June 5, 1990, repatriated under RA 2630 on March 17, 1994, and in 1998 was elected representative of Pangasinan's Second District over Antonio E. Bengson III

The procedural posture: the HRET dismissed Bengson's quo warranto and declared Cruz qualified; Bengson sought certiorari charging grave abuse; the case was originally assigned to Justice Gutierrez (who would have granted the petition), but Justices Kapunan and CJP filed Dissents that prevailed, so Kapunan (the more senior) wrote the ponencia, CJP's dissent became a Concurring Opinion, and the Gutierrez draft became the Dissent

The Kapunan ponencia: citizenship is acquired by birth or naturalization, yielding natural-born and naturalized citizens; under CA 63 a former citizen may reacquire citizenship by naturalization, repatriation, or a direct act of Congress; since Cruz did not undergo naturalization, he 'perforce' is natural-born; the Constitution lists no separate category for reacquirers, who revert to their original classification

CJP's first reason -- repatriation is recovery of ORIGINAL citizenship: citing Jovito Salonga's 'Private International Law' ('recovery of the original nationality') and Webster ('restore to one's country of origin'), repatriation is 'not a grant of a new citizenship, but a recovery of one's former or original citizenship'; doubts in citizenship questions are resolved in the claimant's favor

CJP's second reason -- not naturalized, therefore natural-born: under the present Constitution only two classes of citizens exist; repatriates, not separately classified, reacquire their original status, so Cruz -- 'clearly and concededly not naturalized' -- is natural-born

CJP's third reason -- no grave abuse by the HRET: the Constitution makes the Electoral Tribunals the 'sole judge' of their members' qualifications (Article VI, Section 17); the Court's certiorari power is limited to grave abuse (Co v. HRET; Angara v. Electoral Commission), and a good-faith interpretation of an unsettled question cannot be 'capricious and whimsical' grave abuse (quoting CJP's own Tañada v. Angara)

CJP's fourth reason -- in case of doubt, popular will prevails: Cruz won 80,119 votes, more than all his opponents combined (66,182); 'it would be better to err in favor of the people's choice than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms' (Frivaldo v. Comelec, per Panganiban; Sinaca v. Mula)

CJP's fifth reason -- the trend toward globalization: economically and politically the world is opening its doors; former Filipinos like Cruz, 'Filipinos by blood, by origin and by culture,' are not true aliens, and the country should welcome them back to serve (Cruz was elected mayor within a year of returning)

Justice Gutierrez's Dissent: natural-born status is a privilege conferred on those who needed to do nothing to acquire it; because Cruz had to perform acts (oath, registration, renunciation of US citizenship, affidavit), he did not reacquire natural-born status; the historical trend (1935, 1973, 1987 Constitutions) has made natural-born citizenship 'more narrow and qualified,' and the HRET 'reversed the historical trend and clear intendment'

stances.claim: Repatriation under RA 2630 is the recovery of one's ORIGINAL citizenship, not the grant of a new one; therefore a person who was natural-born before losing his citizenship reacquires natural-born status upon repatriation. Since the Constitution recognizes only two classes -- natural-born and naturalized -- and provides no separate category for reacquirers, and since Cruz was 'clearly and concededly not naturalized,' he is natural-born.
stances.rhetorical_move: definitional dichotomy plus ordinary-meaning: closing the gap (no third category) and grounding 'repatriation = recovery of the original' in lexical and treatise authority (Salonga, Webster)
stances.confidence: the Court's holding (per Kapunan), echoed in CJP's concurrence

stances.claim: The HRET did not commit grave abuse of discretion, because the Constitution makes it the 'sole judge' of its members' qualifications and the Court's certiorari power reaches only capricious, whimsical, despotic action -- not a good-faith interpretation of an unsettled question. 'There is a line between perceived error and grave abuse,' and the Court 'cannot substitute its discretion' for the HRET's.
stances.rhetorical_move: deference-to-constitutional-tribunal: cabining judicial review to grave abuse to respect a co-equal body's exclusive mandate, even where the Court might read the law differently
stances.confidence: asserted by CJP as a controlling limit on review

stances.claim: In case of doubt, the popular will prevails and citizenship doubts are resolved in the claimant's favor -- Cruz won more votes (80,119) than all his opponents combined -- and the global trend favors welcoming back former Filipinos who are 'Filipinos by blood, by origin and by culture'; 'it would be better to err in favor of the people's choice than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms.'
stances.rhetorical_move: popular-will plus globalization framing: layering a democratic tie-breaker and a forward-looking policy rationale onto the legal interpretation

notable_anecdotes: The dissent that became the ruling: the case was first assigned to Justice Gutierrez, who would have unseated Cruz, but Justices Kapunan and CJP filed Dissents that carried the majority -- so Kapunan (the senior) wrote the ponencia, CJP's dissent became a Concurring Opinion, and Gutierrez's draft became the Dissent.

A Marine who came home: Teodoro Cruz lost his natural-born status by enlisting in the US Marine Corps and being naturalized American, then repatriated in 1994 -- and within a year was elected mayor of Mangatarem, and soon after, congressman -- the kind of returning Filipino CJP argued the law should welcome.

Salonga as authority: CJP grounded 'repatriation is the recovery of original citizenship' partly in his mentor Jovito Salonga's treatise 'Private International Law,' which defines repatriation as 'the recovery of the original nationality upon fulfillment of certain conditions.'

The numbers and the will: CJP stressed that Cruz received 80,119 votes -- more than all his opponents combined (66,182) -- invoking the principle that 'it would be better to err in favor of the people's choice than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms.'

The historical-narrowing dissent: Justice Gutierrez surveyed the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions to argue that natural-born citizenship has grown 'more narrow and qualified over the years,' so the HRET had 'reversed the historical trend' by treating a repatriate as natural-born.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'A Centenary of Justice' analyzes Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (GR 142840, May 7, 2001, per Kapunan, J.), which held that repatriation under RA 2630 restores a person's ORIGINAL citizenship. Teodoro C. Cruz, natural-born in 1960, lost his Philippine citizenship by enlisting in the US Marine Corps (1985) and being naturalized American (1990), repatriated in 1994, and in 1998 was elected to the House from Pangasinan's Second District; the HRET dismissed Antonio Bengson III's quo warranto and upheld Cruz, who then charged the tribunal with grave abuse. The Court reasoned that citizenship is acquired by birth or naturalization, yielding only two classes -- natural-born and naturalized -- and since Cruz reacquired his status by repatriation rather than naturalization or a direct act of Congress, he 'perforce' is natural-born, the Constitution providing no separate category for reacquirers. CJP -- whose dissent became a Concurring Opinion after he deferred to the senior Justice Kapunan -- gave five reasons: (1) repatriation is the recovery of original citizenship (citing Salonga's 'Private International Law' and Webster), 'not a grant of a new citizenship'; (2) not being naturalized, Cruz is natural-born; (3) the HRET, as 'sole judge' of its members' qualifications, committed no grave abuse, since a good-faith interpretation of an unsettled question is not capricious or whimsical ('there is a line between perceived error and grave abuse'); (4) in case of doubt the popular will prevails -- Cruz won 80,119 votes, more than all opponents combined -- and 'it would be better to err in favor of the people's choice than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms' (Frivaldo v. Comelec); and (5) the global trend favors welcoming back former Filipinos who are 'Filipinos by blood, by origin and by culture.' Justice Gutierrez dissented, arguing that natural-born status is a privilege that cannot be reacquired once a person must perform acts (oath, renunciation, registration) to regain citizenship, and that the constitutional trend has made natural-born status 'more narrow and qualified over the years.'
